title: Ambiguous Coordinates
statement:
A point was once written as `"(x, y)"`, for example `"(1, 3)"` or `"(2, 0.5)"`. Then its comma, its space and any decimal points were deleted, leaving the string `s`: `"(2, 0.5)"` turned into `"(205)"`. Return every string `"(x, y)"` the point could have been, written with a comma followed by exactly one space, in any order.

Each of `x` and `y` was written in its shortest form:

- The digits are split between `x` and `y`, and each gets at least one.
- A number has at most one decimal point, with at least one digit on each side of it.
- The part before the point (or the whole number, if there is no point) has no leading zero unless it is exactly `"0"`. So `"00"` and `"012"` are not allowed.
- The part after the point does not end in `0`. So `"1.0"` and `"0.10"` are not allowed.

If no reading is possible, return an empty list.
constraints: Every other character of s is a digit
notes:
## Intuition

There are very few places to put the comma (between two digits) and, on each side, few places for a decimal point, so every combination can be listed. The work is deciding which numbers are allowed: a number is legal when its integer part has no leading zero (unless it is just `"0"`) and its fractional part, if any, does not end in `0`. Each side's legal readings are independent, so pair them up.

## Approach

1. Strip the brackets to get `digits`.
2. `readings(part)` lists the legal ways to write `part`: for each `cut`, the first `cut` digits form `whole` and the rest form `fraction` (empty `fraction` means no point).
   - If `whole` has a leading zero and more than one digit, stop: every longer `whole` starts with the same zero.
   - If `fraction` ends in `0`, skip this cut.
   - Otherwise record `whole` or `whole.fraction`.
3. For each `split` from 1 to `digits.length - 1`, combine every reading of the left part (`xs`) with every reading of the right part (`ys`) as `"(x, y)"`.
4. Return `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

`digits = "123"`. With `split = 1`, `xs = ["1"]` and `ys = ["2.3", "23"]`, giving `"(1, 2.3)"` and `"(1, 23)"`. With `split = 2`, `xs = ["1.2", "12"]` and `ys = ["3"]`, giving `"(1.2, 3)"` and `"(12, 3)"`. That is all four answers.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n⁴) for `n = digits.length`: the n - 1 splits produce O(n³) pairs of readings in total, and each string has O(n) characters. With at most 10 digits this is tiny.
- Space: O(n⁴) characters for the output itself; O(n²) extra for one split's readings.

## Pitfalls

- `"0"` alone is a valid integer, but `"00"` and `"01"` are not; `"0.1"` is fine.
- A fractional part ending in `0` (`"1.0"`, `"0.10"`) is never allowed, even when the integer part is valid.
- A point needs a digit before it and after it, so never cut at position 0 or past the last digit when adding one.
- Format exactly as `"(x, y)"` with one space after the comma.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `digits` | `s` without its brackets |
| `readings` | helper returning the legal numbers for a run of digits |
| `cut` | how many digits go before the decimal point |
| `whole`, `fraction` | the digits before and after the point |
| `split` | how many digits go to `x` |
| `xs`, `ys` | legal readings of the left and right parts |
| `result` | every coordinate string found |

narration.2: Drop the brackets; only the digits matter.
narration.3: A helper that lists every legal way to write one run of digits as a number.
narration.5: Try putting the decimal point after cut digits; cut equal to the length means no point.
narration.7: The digits after the point (empty when there is no point).
narration.8: A multi-digit integer part starting with 0 is illegal, and so is every longer one: stop.
narration.9: A fractional part ending in 0 has an extra zero: skip it.
narration.10: Record the number, with a point only if there is a fractional part.
narration.15: Choose how many digits belong to x; both sides need at least one.
narration.16: All legal readings of the left part.
narration.17: All legal readings of the right part.
narration.20: Format the pair with a comma and one space.
narration.24: Every split and every pair of readings has been listed.
